Medical Educators Outline Framework to Safeguard Physician Training in Artificial Intelligence Era

Medical educators representing the Society of General Internal Medicine have published a comprehensive position paper establishing a formal framework for integrating artificial intelligence technologies into clinical training while protecting essential physician competencies. Approved by the society’s council on June 12, 2026, and published in the Journal of General Internal Medicine, the guidance directly addresses the rapid adoption of large language models across medical schools and residency programs following their initial broad availability in 2022. Although generative tools exhibit extensive capabilities for medical information synthesis and content drafting, surveys cited in the report demonstrate that a majority of trainees report inadequate knowledge regarding the fundamental capabilities and operational boundaries of these algorithms. Because internal medicine functions primarily as an intellectually driven, cognitive discipline, the authors emphasize that uncritical reliance on automated outputs threatens to erode clinical problem-solving, undermine diagnostic proficiency, and fundamentally weaken the physician-patient relationship unless systematic educational safeguards are instituted.

The position paper identifies a specific triad of developmental hazards confronting trainees who engage with automated systems: never-skilling, de-skilling, and mis-skilling. Never-skilling occurs when novice clinicians bypass the cognitive labor essential for developing foundational critical thinking and diagnostic synthesis by prematurely outsourcing their reasoning to automated platforms. Without establishing baseline clinical competencies, these learners become acutely vulnerable to automation bias, deferring uncritically to algorithmic outputs even when recommendations contain hazardous clinical errors. In contrast, de-skilling affects seasoned practitioners who already possess baseline mastery but suffer progressive skill decay through continuous cognitive offloading. The authors highlight documentation of technical degradation following automated tool adoption in procedural domains such as colonoscopy, noting that severe skill decay reduces the practitioner’s supervisory capacity to a performative gesture. Mis-skilling represents the internalization of flawed reasoning or algorithmic hallucinations, embedding erroneous diagnostic scripts and systemic biases regarding race, gender, or disease presentations permanently into the clinician’s cognitive framework.

To navigate these vulnerabilities, the position paper establishes a three-tier taxonomy that categorizes clinical activities by their inherent procedural variability, potential clinical risk, and suitability for automation. Tasks classified as automation-appropriate represent high-volume, low-variability administrative and clerical processes that carry clear objective outcomes and historically high rates of clerical error. Examples within this tier include billing and coding reconciliation, diagnostic code indexing, basic information retrieval, and structured coordination tasks such as prior authorization workflows and referral routing. For these routine responsibilities, training programs are urged to redirect instruction away from independent manual execution toward structured system supervision, failure recognition, and exception management. By delegating low-risk, repetitive responsibilities to automated tools, educational institutions and clinical systems can diminish burdensome documentation overhead, thereby releasing physician attention and instructional hours for direct human care and advanced diagnostic interpretation.

The intermediate category within the taxonomy encompasses hybrid tasks, characterized by moderate to high clinical complexity containing discrete elements that benefit from automated assistance alongside critical steps requiring direct professional oversight. Common clinical illustrations include utilizing algorithmic platforms to draft patient portal responses that clinicians must independently contextualize and approve, deploying ambient documentation systems subject to clinician auditing, and integrating structured analytical prompts into diagnostic deliberations. The authors stress that effective human-artificial intelligence collaboration is not synonymous with passive endorsement; rather, it demands active critical appraisal, real-time verification, and deliberate refinement or rejection of computational outputs. Because hybrid responsibilities present immediate exposure to both never-skilling and de-skilling, they necessitate novel instructional methodologies that compel trainees to engage analytically with algorithmic recommendations rather than accepting synthesized suggestions as complete clinical assessments.

At the opposite end of the spectrum lie automation-resistant or human-only responsibilities, encompassing clinical encounters marked by significant diagnostic variability, elevated stakes, and profound interpersonal nuance. These activities include navigating end-of-life choices, addressing intricate medical uncertainty amid contradictory diagnostic data, and weaving individual patient values and cultural preferences into tailored care management strategies. The authors explain that these interactions demand emotional intelligence, autobiographical memory, and somatic markers developed through direct human connection that computational systems cannot possess. The paper cites clinical evidence showing that empathetic interpersonal communication expands patient disclosure, that strong therapeutic alliances independently correlate with enhanced treatment adherence, and that sustained continuity of physician care reduces patient mortality. Furthermore, automated platforms exhibit systematic vulnerabilities in moral reasoning, demonstrating instability when prompt framing shifts, which makes unmediated algorithmic judgment a direct hazard during ethical deliberations.

To safeguard foundational competency development, the authors urge medical educators to institute formal competency thresholds through specialized Entrustable Professional Activities mapped to existing accreditation frameworks. Trainees should be required to demonstrate verified independent mastery in clinical reasoning before receiving access to automated decision-support software in patient-care environments. Under this staged model, basic competencies must be verified prior to utilizing computational drafting tools, whereas advanced diagnostic synthesis must be solidly established before learners can consult algorithmic engines for differential diagnosis formulation. Educational programs are advised to embed deliberate cognitive safeguards into instructional modules, such as structured think-first exercises requiring learners to write out initial diagnostic impressions and therapeutic plans prior to inspecting computational suggestions. This sequential structure prevents premature offloading and preserves the mental friction necessary for building durable cognitive schemas.

Addressing the preservation of long-term skills, the guidance recommends differentiating between automated tools operating in answer-delivery mode and those configured in learning mode. While answer-delivery platforms supply immediate conclusions that eliminate necessary intellectual struggle, learning-mode applications introduce intentional pedagogical friction by posing reflective prompts that compel trainees to reason through clinical steps before reviewing answers. Curricula must also incorporate deliberate practice opportunities within simulated settings specifically engineered to expose algorithmic errors, false positive associations, and subtle diagnostic misdirections.
